​At the core of BeamNG.drive is its proprietary soft-body physics engine, which replaced rigid-body physics traditionally used in video games.
​Nodes and Beams Architecture: Every vehicle is constructed from a vast web of microscopic \"nodes\" (mass points) connected by \"beams\" (spring-like elements with properties like elasticity, strength, and deformation limits).
​Real-Time Stress Calculation: When a car impacts an obstacle, the engine calculates real-time stress across thousands of individual beams. If a beam exceeds its yield strength, it bends permanently; if it exceeds its ultimate strength, it snaps.
​Complex Material Behavior: Materials aren't just uniform metal sheets. The physics model distinguishes between frame rails, thin body panels, glass (which shatters dynamically), rubber tires, and suspension arms, causing realistic buckling, twisting, and crumpling.
​2. Crash Physics @COMMENT_BODY@ Mechanical Simulation
​BeamNG doesn't just look like it's crashing; it simulates the internal mechanical forces causing the crash.
​Full Powertrain Simulation: The engine models internal combustion mechanics down to individual pistons, valves, and turbochargers. Overrevving an engine can float valves or throw a rod; punching a hole in the oil pan causes oil starvation and engine seizure.
​Drivetrain @COMMENT_BODY@ Suspension Dynamics: Driveshafts can twist and snap under high torque, differentials lock or break realistically, and suspension geometry changes dynamically as control arms bend.
​Tire Physics @COMMENT_BODY@ Aerodynamics: Tires experience realistic deflation, sidewall flexing, and temperature/pressure changes. Airflow creates dynamic downforce and drag, meaning a missing door or crumpled hood alters how the car handles mid-flight.

​Powered by a heavily modified version of the Torque3D engine, BeamNG pairs its heavy-duty physics with impressive visual and environmental fidelity.Feature Details

Environments Massive open-world maps ranging from dense urban cities and tight mountain passes (like East Coast USA or Utah) to rugged off-road trails and stunt arenas.
Particle @COMMENT_BODY@ Surface Effects Dynamic tire smoke, dust plumes, mud accumulation, sparks from metal scraping against asphalt, and realistic water physics.
Sound Design Audio is tightly synchronized with mechanical stress—screeching tires, groaning chassis frames, supercharger whines, and crunching metal change pitch and intensity based on velocity and deformation.4. Gameplay, Modes, and Sandbox Freedom

​Free Roam @COMMENT_BODY@ Traffic AI: Spawn anywhere on any map, place traffic cars controlled by intelligent AI, and simulate police pursuits or highway pile-ups.
​Scenarios @COMMENT_BODY@ Time Trials: Precision driving challenges, delivery missions, high-speed jumps, and stunt courses.
​Career Mode: An expanding role-playing mode where players buy vehicles, manage repair costs, take on transport jobs, and build up a garage from scratch.

## Objective
- Build a complete, playable driving game inspired by BeamNG.drive, featuring car customization, dynamic weather and time, quests, and multiplayer-style activity.

## Requirements
- Add famous car brands and distinct engine sounds; customization for paint, spoilers, turbo stages, and tires.
- Add quests, activity jobs, rewards, and online multiplayer where players can connect and ram each other.
- Include morning/night cycles and weather such as snow, rain, tornadoes, flash floods, frost, and volcanoes.
- Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and briefly note them at completion.

## Decisions
- Built a self-contained browser game with original vehicle names and canvas-based driving visuals.
- Implemented a local browser-tab room link rather than claiming real worldwide multiplayer; the UI explicitly notes the limitation.

## Work State
### Completed
- Created a playable driving scene with keyboard/touch controls, speed and integrity HUD, traffic obstacles, collision damage, and a canyon route.
- Added a nine-car garage, upgrades/customization, weather and time controls, contracts, daily challenge, map panel, and engine-tone sound synthesis.
- Added a driver lobby using `BroadcastChannel` for same-browser-tab room signaling.
- Added responsive UI and pause controls.
- `node --check game.js` passed.

### Active
- Validate the game in a browser and fix any runtime/UI issues.
- Confirm the local server is running and capture/inspect a screenshot.

### Blocked
- Browser check failed because `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` returned `net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`; the project start script defaults to port `3000`, not `3002`.
- The browser was initially unavailable; Chromium was installed successfully with `playwright-cli install-browser chromium`.

## Next Move
1. Start the project server on port `3000` (or explicitly set `PORT=3002`) and verify the endpoint.
2. Open it with `playwright-cli`, inspect the rendered game, and save/read the latest screenshot.
3. Test key interactions, especially garage purchasing, customization, weather/time, quests, pause/resume, and lobby.
4. Address any discovered issues and report multiplayer limitations and other assumptions.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and HUD.
- `styles.css`: Game visuals and responsive styling.
- `game.js`: Canvas simulation, controls, game state, quests, customization, weather, and room signaling.
- `start.sh`: Project start command.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted.
- The start script invokes the runtime’s default server, which uses port `3000` unless `PORT` is set.
- Lobby messaging uses `BroadcastChannel`; it is not an internet-connected multiplayer server, and ramming between remote players is not implemented.

## Objective
- Build a complete, playable browser driving game inspired by BeamNG.drive, with customizable cars, weather and time options, contracts, and multiplayer-style activity.

## Requirements
- Include famous car brands, distinct engine sounds, paint, spoilers, turbo stages, and tire customization.
- Add quests, jobs, rewards, and online multiplayer where players can connect and ram each other.
- Include morning/night cycles and clear weather, snow, rain, tornadoes, flash floods, frost, and volcanoes.
- Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and briefly note them at completion.

## Decisions
- Built a self-contained canvas browser game with original vehicle/model names and synthesized engine tones.
- Lobby uses `BroadcastChannel` for local browser-tab room signaling; the UI discloses that worldwide matchmaking and driver collision interactions are not connected.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented the driving scene, keyboard/touch controls, speed and integrity HUD, traffic/cone obstacles, collision damage, and a canyon route.
- Added nine car choices, garage unlocks, paint/spoiler/turbo/tire customization, weather/time controls, contracts, daily challenge, map panel, and pause/resume.
- Added local driver room signaling and responsive layout.
- `node --check game.js` passed.
- Started the project server; `http://localhost:3000` responds successfully.
- Opened the game in Playwright. Page rendered with expected HUD and no JavaScript console errors; only a missing `/favicon.ico` 404 was reported.

### Active
- Fix and validate remaining interaction issues, then capture and inspect a screenshot.
- Test garage purchases, customization, weather/time, quests, pause/resume, and lobby behavior.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Capture a small JPEG screenshot of the current browser view and inspect it.
2. Exercise key game interactions in Playwright; fix any issues found.
3. Re-run `node --check game.js` and report the game plus the local-only multiplayer limitation and other assumptions.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface, HUD, modal and pause overlays.
- `styles.css`: Visual styling and responsive layout.
- `game.js`: Canvas simulation, controls, game state, quests, customization, weather/time, and lobby signaling.
- `start.sh`: Project start command.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; new files include `index.html`, `styles.css`, and `game.js`.
- The server defaults to port `3000`; port `3002` refused connections.
- Multiplayer is not an internet-connected server, and ramming between remote players is not implemented.

## Torque Valley is ready to play

The browser game is implemented in `index.html`, `styles.css`, and `game.js`. It includes a canyon driving scene with keyboard and touch controls, traffic and obstacles, collision damage, a garage with nine car choices, paint and tuning options, weather and time settings, contracts, a daily challenge, and pause/resume.

**Controls:** WASD or arrow keys to drive; Space for the handbrake. Touch controls are available on mobile.

**Multiplayer limitation:** Room signaling works between Torque Valley tabs in the same browser context. There’s no internet-connected matchmaking or player-to-player collision.

I made the reasonable assumption that this should be a self-contained browser prototype, using original vehicle names and synthesized engine sounds. I validated the main UI interactions and driving in the browser; `node --check game.js` passed, and the final reload showed no console errors. The project files are currently uncommitted.
